newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexican markets shrug off PRI meeting.
newsitem.headline: Mexican markets shrug off PRI meeting.

text.p: Mexican financial markets on Monday paid little attention to this past weekend's landmark assembly of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI), analysts and traders said.

Instead, other factors such as speculation over U.S. interest rates led to slumping share prices on the Mexican stock exchange, a shaky peso and higher interest rates on the secondary money market, they said.
The PRI held a key plenary assembly this weekend in a rare opportunity to see internal party politicking played out in public.

Among other decisions, the party decided that future presidential candidates must have previously held elective office, a decision that disqualified "technocrats" like current President Ernesto Zedillo.

The party also condemned Zedillo's intention to privatize a petrochemical unit of the government oil monopoly Pemex as a series of speakers railed against free-market policies and called for an "authentic nationalist, revolutionary spirit" and a return to the party's leftist roots.
But analysts said they were expecting little real change.

"I don't think this has had much impact on the market," said Santos Herrera, an analyst with the Estrategia Bursatil brokerage. "In fact, what there might be in the future is reaction to the move against the petrochemical privatization.
"There wasn't a lot that happened," he added. "A lot needs to be defined and basically there were short-term decisions focused on the 1997 elections."
Traders in the secondary Cetes and peso markets said they considered the weekend assembly little more than a standard political event.
"It was more of the same," one Cetes trader said. "The markets weren't changed by it. It won't have any effect."

Aside from speculation over whether the U.S. Federal Reserve's Open Market Committee will raise interest rates on Tuesday, recent Mexican economic data are driving the markets, analyst said. "It's not going to be an easy week for the markets," said
Rodolfo Campuzano, an analyst with the de Invex brokerage. "Apart from what's happening with the Fed, people didn't like much the drop in the (Mexican) trade surplus."

The government's preliminary trade figures for August showed that Mexico's trade surplus fell to $264 million, way below market expectations. A Reuters survey of 11 analysts MXAAP forecast the August trade surplus at $435 million.

Moreover, the same survey is predicting the Consumer Price Index will rise by 0.97 percent for the first half of September, which could be driving up interest rates. The government is due to make the inflation announcement on Tuesday.
"Higher rates are expected in the primary Cetes (auction) tomorrow," Campuzano said.
